key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged users set autopay only slightly above the minimum and some lost automatic payment protection entirely.
methodology: Field experiment (RCT) on live credit card accounts with 6-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's central question in the right setting: a consumer financial-product nudge changed nominal enrollment/behavior without moving the outcome that matters (debt/savings amount), and worsened outcomes for liquidity-constrained users — the strongest evidence for the support team's 'vanity enrolment' worry.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
single nudge design (shrouding), not a direct opt-in/opt-out/active-choice comparison
relevance_reason: On-domain consumer financial nudge study showing default/nudge effects on nominal behavior diverge from substantive outcomes, directly contradicting the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: A state-of-the-art narrative overview of how DC plan design (auto-enrollment, default investments, framing) affects participation, contribution, and portfolio choice, including negative engagement effects.
methodology: Narrative review/overview of the DC retirement plan literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a broad, up-to-date map of what is known about defaults in employer plans, useful as background but not decision-specific since it never addresses consumer, self-directed, liquid-savings settings.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
narrative rather than systematic synthesis with pooled effect sizes
relevance_reason: Recent survey of the analogous employer-plan default literature; useful background but off the brief's actual setting.

key_finding: Argues that default enrollment in US retirement plans raises short-term participation but induces long-term passivity (low contribution anchoring, account churn) unless paired with auto-escalation and reminders.
methodology: Narrative/opinion synthesis, no new data. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Restates a point already made more rigorously by other papers in this set (e.g. Choukhmane, Choi et al.), adding little new evidence for the enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off.
limitations: employer retirement setting, not consumer fintech
no original data, low-citation venue
no quantified effect sizes
relevance_reason: Restates the passivity concern the brief already raises, but with no new evidence beyond stronger papers already in the set.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for 'downstream' default effects, showing default effects on later consumer behavior depend on time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and are inconsistent across studies.
methodology: Theoretical review/conceptual synthesis (taxonomy and framework), Consumer Psychology Review. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the moderator variables (time course, prior preferences, salience) that should shape how we measure persistence at 6-12 months and who a default helps versus hurts — directly usable as a measurement checklist rather than a design choice.
limitations: conceptual/taxonomic, not a quantitative meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: The clearest on-domain review of when and why default effects persist or fade downstream, filling the brief's request for a synthesis paper.

key_finding: Using natural experiments with random assignment to default options in Medicare Part D, beneficiary passivity toward defaults is large, persistent, and strikingly insensitive to how bad the default option is; active-choice variation looks driven by transitory attention shocks rather than stable attentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments, including random assignment to default plan options, on Medicare Part D administrative data.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that people do not self-correct out of bad defaults even when it costs them materially — a caution against assuming a good default choice will be actively corrected if wrong, and evidence that 'active choosers' are not a stable, identifiable segment.
limitations: health insurance/drug plan setting, not a consumer financial savings product
no employer- or app-based enrollment mechanism comparable to ours
relevance_reason: Closest non-employer analogue on default persistence and the limits of active choice, though the domain (health insurance) is not the brief's financial-product setting.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise by only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs from escalation are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalation defaults escalate on the first scheduled date.
methodology: Administrative data analysis across nine 401(k) plans, incorporating turnover and withdrawal dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement that measured default effects shrink substantially once medium/long-run attrition and opt-out are accounted for — directly relevant to the brief's question of whether a default's enrollment lift survives 6-12 months, though in a locked-plan setting.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated enrollment, mechanism does not carry over per the brief
relevance_reason: Strongest quantified contradiction of 'defaults always help' in the employer-plan analogy literature, but capped for being off the brief's consumer-app setting.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most affected individuals actively opted back out, with the default effect strongest among those with high incentives and low awareness of their enrollment status.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and linked survey data around a nationwide auto-enrollment policy change.
why_it_matters: Shows a large headline enrollment effect can coexist with widespread active opt-out, and that the effect concentrates among the least-informed — relevant to the distributional concern that defaults can help those who did not need it least and confuse others.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension, not a consumer app
government-mediated rather than self-directed fintech enrollment
relevance_reason: Recent large-scale default-vs-opt-out evidence with heterogeneity by knowledge/incentive, but in a public pension rather than consumer setting.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, with only modest average savings increases though a significant reduction in savings inequality; a life-cycle model estimates the effective switching cost at about $250.
methodology: Panel analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's question about whether default enrollment gains persist at 6-12+ months — they attenuate by medium-run horizons — but in a locked retirement-savings context rather than liquid consumer savings.
limitations: retirement plan setting, employer/national-scheme mediated
structural model estimates rely on modeling assumptions about switching costs
relevance_reason: Best available quantification of medium-run attenuation of default effects, the exact persistence question the brief asks, though off the brief's consumer-app setting.

key_finding: In three experiments (including a representative five-country European sample, n=4207), default nudges strongly shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but a default nudge — and especially a refused default — lowers users' rating of the advice received, mediated by perceived wealth-manager honesty; how the default is framed and presented also shifts the amount invested.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country EU sample, on default nudges in investment/advice settings.
why_it_matters: Directly informs both open decisions: it shows a preset level's framing can anchor the amount chosen, and it gives EU consumer evidence on exactly when a default starts to read as manipulative and damage trust — the reputational risk the brief flags.
limitations: investment/wealth-management context rather than round-up savings specifically
no 6-12 month persistence measure, single-session experiments
relevance_reason: EU consumer-financial experimental evidence directly on framing/anchoring of default levels and on perceived manipulation, matching the brief's regulatory concern almost exactly.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment pushed 401(k) participation above 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still had not moved off the default after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset level anchors most participants near the default rather than their preferred level for years — the classic result the newer, more relevant literature is arguing with.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, foundational/older work the brief says the app context has since outgrown
no consumer fintech or liquid-savings analogue
relevance_reason: The canonical anchoring-on-default-level result; useful as the baseline the current, more relevant papers react against, but not itself decision-changing for this project.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (friction complementarity), and a counterfactual added menu option captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at only 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million real transactions plus an independent stated-preference survey of preferences.
why_it_matters: Gives a rigorous, transferable method for reasoning about the round-up multiplier menu decision: how a preset level's design trades off consumer welfare against provider revenue, and how much of default adherence is genuine preference versus friction — directly useful for choosing and defending the 1x/2x/5x menu.
limitations: tipping decisions on a ride-hailing app, not a savings product
one-shot payment choice rather than an enrolled, ongoing savings behavior
relevance_reason: A methodologically strong consumer digital-choice-architecture study whose menu-design and welfare-cost framework transfers directly to the round-up multiplier decision.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term, liquid, withdrawable savings account offered via UK employer payroll saw take-up of at most 0.7% of eligible employees, but among those who opted in, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a payroll-deduction short-term savings program introduced at five UK firms, with 12-month account-level tracking.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world analogue to the brief's product (liquid, withdrawable savings, opt-in): it shows opt-in take-up can be extremely low while retention among adopters is excellent, directly bearing on the opt-in-vs-opt-out trade-off, though the employer-payroll channel is not our app.
limitations: employer payroll-mediated enrollment, not a standalone consumer app
very low opt-in sample may limit generalizability of retention statistics
relevance_reason: Rare evidence on a liquid, short-term savings product (not retirement) under opt-in, directly speaking to the brief's enrolment-vs-engagement trade-off despite the employer channel.

key_finding: Characterizes when opt-out-minimizing versus opt-out-maximizing default designs are welfare-optimal, showing weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal when designer and choosers agree on the activity's value, with extensions to externalities, Pigouvian fees, and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical economic model with asymptotic characterization, validated via numerical simulation.
why_it_matters: Offers a welfare-optimization lens for thinking about who a default should target and how aggressively, useful for reasoning about the distributional trade-off, but abstract and not grounded in any consumer or financial-product data.
limitations: purely theoretical/simulation-based, no empirical population
no specific setting stated, so applicability to a round-up savings feature is inferred rather than demonstrated
relevance_reason: General welfare theory of optimal default design that could frame the distributional trade-off, but too abstract to directly settle either open decision.

key_finding: EU dark-pattern law protects biased consumers under an autonomy lens; the paper builds a taxonomy of six categories of autonomy violations to classify when pre-selected defaults and similar choice-architecture practices become regulable dark patterns.
methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis mapping EU laws addressing dark patterns and proposing a normative classification; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the EU regulatory framework for distinguishing a helpful opt-out default from a legally and reputationally risky dark pattern, directly bearing on the entry-design decision's compliance exposure.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical
no effect sizes on enrolment or savings behavior
general online choice architecture, not a round-up savings feature specifically
relevance_reason: Provides the EU legal taxonomy for when a pre-selected default crosses into a dark pattern, central to the brief's reputational-risk concern.

key_finding: A 12% default contribution rate retained 25% of employees after 12 months (versus ~50% for lower defaults in prior literature), with many staying at 12% despite it being a likely suboptimal rate, especially among lower-income employees.
methodology: Observational analysis of employer retirement-plan enrollment data with literature comparison; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that a high preset default can anchor a large share of users at a level that may not suit their means, informing the risk of pre-selecting the highest round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not consumer self-directed liquid savings
no engagement or withdrawal data beyond 12 months
relevance_reason: Strongest available evidence on anchoring effects of a high preset default level, though in an employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted/unavailable; title indicates UK field experiments automating short-term payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only (text unavailable/garbled).
why_it_matters: Potentially directly relevant to automatic enrollment into short-term savings, but no usable evidence can be extracted from the available abstract.
limitations: abstract text is corrupted and provides no extractable findings
relevance_reason: Title suggests strong relevance, but no usable evidence is present in the record.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in market-wide annual savings, though achieving less than half of the potential avoidable savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks; abstract-only for statistics.
why_it_matters: The closest real consumer-banking analog of automatic enrollment producing measurable behavioral savings, setting a benchmark for what an opt-out round-up design could realistically achieve and its shortfall from the ceiling.
limitations: studies overdraft alerts, not savings contributions
no data on enrollment persistence or engagement depth over 6-12 months for the feature itself
relevance_reason: A large-scale UK consumer-bank field experiment on automatic enrollment gives a directly comparable effect-size benchmark in the same industry and regulatory environment.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment raised savings by £32-38/month but was partially offset by increases in unsecured debt (~£7/month) and higher mortgage balances over 41 months, even as loan defaults fell and credit scores rose modestly.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment following UK automatic-enrollment roll-out across ~160,000 small employers; observational, longitudinal (41 months).
why_it_matters: Challenges the assumption that auto-enrollment-driven savings represent unambiguous net financial improvement, relevant to whether round-up balances represent genuine new saving or are offset elsewhere.
limitations: employer-mediated pension context, not consumer self-directed liquid savings
abstract gives raw monetary figures without percentage effect sizes
relevance_reason: Longitudinal evidence that automatic-enrollment savings gains can be offset by debt increases, a caution against treating enrollment numbers as pure benefit.

key_finding: Removing an auto-enrollment default and adding an application "ordeal" reduced health-insurance enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people, undermining the standard efficiency rationale for ordeals in selection markets.
methodology: Natural experiment analyzing removal of an auto-enrollment policy in a public health-insurance program; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shows friction added to a formerly automatic process can produce large, distributionally skewed enrollment drops, cautioning against treating opt-in as a neutral, low-cost alternative to opt-out.
limitations: public health-insurance selection market, not a consumer financial savings product
relevance_reason: Quantifies how much friction reduces enrollment and who is disproportionately excluded, informative for weighing opt-in versus opt-out risk of excluding vulnerable users.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not adjust the amount they donated to compensate.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting different roll-out timing of prechecked recurring-donation boxes across 2020 U.S. campaign websites; large-scale transaction data.
why_it_matters: A directly analogous consumer digital-choice-architecture default shows real enrollment gains alongside real regret/withdrawal signals concentrated among inexperienced users — the closest empirical evidence for the support team's disengagement and complaint concern about opt-out enrollment.
limitations: political donations, not savings behavior
no direct long-term retention measure beyond refund requests
U.S. setting, not EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: Quantified evidence of both the enrollment-boosting power and distributional harm of a pre-checked recurring default in a real consumer digital product, closely mirroring the round-up feature's opt-out risk.

key_finding: In lab search experiments, a default option raises reservation utility via a reference effect and improves choice quality, while people with higher reservation utility self-select into actively searching for better options.
methodology: Laboratory choice experiments testing a reference-dependent search model; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a general behavioral mechanism for how defaults interact with search, but does not speak to enrollment rates, persistence, or consumer financial products.
limitations: abstract lab experiment unrelated to financial enrollment decisions
no connection to savings amounts or contribution levels
relevance_reason: Tangential behavioral-economics evidence on defaults and search, included for completeness but not decision-relevant.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with the effect still visible 15+ months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences analysis of the real-world DMA rollout across iOS and Android devices; large-scale usage data.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale, EU-regulatory, persistence-tested evidence on how forced/active choice compares to defaults — directly informs whether an active-choice onboarding step for the round-up feature would produce durable behavior change rather than a one-off bump.
limitations: mobile browser choice, not a financial savings product
does not measure amount saved or contribution levels
relevance_reason: A real EU regulatory active-choice intervention with quantified, persistent effects — the strongest available evidence for the active-choice comparison criterion.

key_finding: In a usability study with 410 participants testing nine opt-out interface designs for privacy choices, generalizing individual opt-out choices to broader categories slightly reduced opt-out utility but greatly increased efficiency and reduced disruption, with 98% of participants feeling undisrupted under the least disruptive scheme.
methodology: Design and usability study using a browser-extension prototype tested by 410 participants.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates concrete, tested UI patterns for implementing an active-choice, no-default flow with low friction, directly useful for designing the round-up feature's active-choice onboarding or level-entry field.
limitations: privacy opt-out domain under US law (CCPA/GPC), not financial enrollment
no measure of downstream financial engagement or savings behavior
relevance_reason: Offers a concrete, tested design pattern for implementing active choice without a default, relevant to how the entry/level UI could be built.

key_finding: Field experiments changing university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-up uptake in all cases, but for outcomes requiring effort, completion and passing improved only in the single-exam case with stronger default endorsement, and only among previously "responsive" students; non-responsive students showed higher sign-up but no real behavior change.
methodology: Two field experiments changing default enrollment procedures for university exam registration; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the support team's core worry that a default only inflates nominal enrollment without changing the effortful downstream behavior that follows, and shows this happens precisely for less-responsive individuals.
limitations: university exam sign-up setting, not a consumer financial product
heterogeneity defined by past university responsiveness, not directly transferable to banking-app user segments
relevance_reason: The closest available evidence that opt-out defaults can inflate nominal enrollment without changing effortful downstream behavior for some segments, mirroring the vanity-enrollment concern.

key_finding: After a policy change allowed target-date funds as default retirement investments, younger and older workers' stock allocations shifted in line with the TDF glidepath default, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act's default-option provision.
why_it_matters: Suggests a default can strongly anchor an allocation/level choice while leaving a related but distinct behavior (contribution amount) largely unaffected, informative for whether a preset multiplier would anchor the level chosen without changing whether people save.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement investment context, not consumer self-directed liquid savings
measures asset allocation rather than a directly analogous round-up multiplier choice
relevance_reason: Evidence that a default anchors the specific dimension it targets while leaving adjacent behavior largely unaffected, informative for the anchoring question.

key_finding: In an RCT with 220 participants, all tested nudges - including default options - significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings relative to a control group, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (N=220) testing social norms, framing, default options, and narrative nudges on Chinese voluntary pension-saving decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise enrollment or contribution, a rare empirical counter-example the brief explicitly asked us to weigh against the 'defaults always help' assumption.
limitations: small online survey sample (n=220) measuring stated willingness rather than real financial behavior
Chinese cultural/institutional context differs from an EU consumer app
voluntary pension product rather than a liquid consumer savings app
relevance_reason: The clearest available contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise, directly answering the brief's explicit request for counter-evidence.

key_finding: People generally approve of financial nudges/interventions, rating them positively on approval, benefit, ethics and likelihood-of-use (with manipulation reverse-coded), with stronger approval for System-2-style and savings-framed interventions regardless of whether a bank is the messenger.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment with 2,100 representative Australian respondents shown 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing and System type.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether consumers perceive bank-issued savings nudges as manipulative or acceptable, which is the reputational/dark-pattern risk the brief flags for the entry-design decision.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios rather than an actual enrolment decision
Australian sample, not EU
no measurement of enrolment or amount saved
relevance_reason: Provides direct consumer evidence on perceived manipulativeness of bank-proposed savings nudges, informing C5.

key_finding: Offering conditional-cash-transfer recipients a choice of delivery method produced no significant average impact on overall savings, though it raised balances for those with initially nonpositive balances.
methodology: Randomized offering of delivery-method choice to CCT beneficiaries; abstract-only detail.
why_it_matters: Shows a choice-architecture change did not move aggregate savings amounts, a caution against assuming any design tweak lifts real savings.
limitations: developing-country cash-transfer population, not a fintech consumer app
measures delivery-method choice rather than an enrolment default
no effect sizes in abstract
relevance_reason: Offers a limited/null result on whether choice architecture changes amount saved rather than just nominal status.

key_finding: Compares automatic-IRA program variants that share identical contribution amounts and liquid-fund features, but the truncated abstract gives no quantified wealth effect.
methodology: abstract-only; comparison of program design variants.
why_it_matters: Touches the liquid-emergency-savings angle relevant to a round-up feature but provides too little substance to inform either decision.
limitations: abstract is truncated and uninformative
auto-IRA is a state/employer-mediated program, not a consumer app
no effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Nominally about automatic enrolment with a liquid-savings component, but lacks usable findings.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment dramatically raised participation, and many employees stuck with the default contribution rate and fund allocation for years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from one large U.S. corporation before and after a switch to automatic enrolment.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration of the default participation effect and level-anchoring mechanism, useful as a benchmark even though the employer setting differs from ours.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app
no analysis of the employer-trust mechanism's absence in our setting
single-firm study
relevance_reason: Classic evidence for both the default participation effect (C1) and default-level anchoring (C3).

key_finding: No findings available; abstract is missing.
methodology: abstract-only; content unknown.
why_it_matters: Title suggests a direct auto-vs-voluntary enrolment comparison but without an abstract it cannot inform any decision.
limitations: no abstract provided
employer-sponsored DC plan setting
relevance_reason: Potentially relevant title but no usable content.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority/non-national status are associated with both under-saving and early withdrawal of retirement savings, putting the same individuals at risk on both margins.
methodology: Analysis of three nationally representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension-freedom reform.
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the support team's worry — that low-trust or vulnerable users could be the ones who withdraw and complain even as headline enrolment looks good.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
Estonian institutional context differs from general EU banking-app users
early-withdrawal option differs from round-up withdrawal mechanics
relevance_reason: Provides distributional evidence on who is helped versus hurt by savings defaults and who withdraws early, relevant to C5.

key_finding: Prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrolment policy reduced stated intentions and approval, showing that making a default salient can trigger backlash.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment (n=24,303) across G7 countries testing reflection prompts about a hypothetical default policy.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that awareness of being defaulted-in can backfire and reduce approval, a caution relevant to the reputational/dark-pattern risk of opt-out enrolment.
limitations: public-health/vaccination setting, not a financial product
hypothetical rather than an actual enrolment decision
measures stated intentions/approval, not enrolment or amount
relevance_reason: Rare evidence that salience of a default can backfire, informing the manipulation/reputational-risk criterion.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment and employer matching are associated with higher retirement-plan participation among U.S. Millennials.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study survey.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the well-established default-participation effect in a modern cohort but adds little beyond stronger existing causal evidence and stays in the employer-plan setting.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
cross-sectional/associational, no causal design
no quantified effect size beyond association
relevance_reason: Additional confirmation of the default-participation link, replaceable by stronger causal studies already present.

key_finding: Automatic (passive) contributions raise wealth accumulation substantially while active-choice subsidies raise total saving by only about 1 cent per dollar, because roughly 85% of individuals are passive savers unresponsive to subsidies but strongly moved by defaults.
methodology: Administrative panel of 41 million observations on Danish savings comparing active-choice subsidy policies to passive automatic-contribution policies.
why_it_matters: The strongest large-sample distributional split of active versus passive savers, informing which users would actually be affected by defaulting everyone into round-ups.
limitations: retirement/tax-advantaged accounts in Denmark's pension system, not a liquid consumer app
compares subsidies vs automatic contributions, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice as defined here
no discussion of employer-trust mechanism absence in our setting
relevance_reason: Provides the strongest distributional evidence on who defaults help versus leave unaffected, relevant to C5.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' meaningfully changes behavior relative to no intervention, and a novel 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option can approach the effectiveness of automatic enrolment.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments comparing opt-out defaults, plain active choice, and enhanced active choice on behavior-change outcomes.
why_it_matters: Directly answers whether active choice can capture most of the enrolment benefit of a default without an opt-out, exactly the comparison the brief needs for the entry-design decision, and proposes a concrete design to test.
limitations: field experiments are in medication adherence and general savings contexts, not a round-up banking app
older study (2011), predates current fintech/regulatory context
abstract does not fully quantify enhanced-active-choice effect sizes
relevance_reason: The origin study of active choice and enhanced active choice as an alternative to opt-out defaults, the mechanism the entry decision needs evidence on (C6).

key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance evidence on how choice architecture, product design, defaults, and disclosure shape savings and other financial decisions, situating default effects among a broader intervention toolkit.
methodology: Narrative review/NBER chapter summarizing empirical regularities and intervention evidence in household finance.
why_it_matters: Provides the review-level synthesis of choice-architecture and default evidence the brief asked for, giving broader context for benchmarking both design decisions.
limitations: broad overview rather than a study with its own effect sizes
covers household finance generally, not round-up savings or EU fintech specifically
synthesizes largely employer-plan and classic literature
relevance_reason: Supplies the review/meta-level synthesis of default and choice-architecture evidence the brief explicitly wants represented.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment raised 401(k) participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants (half even after three years) stuck with the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, roughly offsetting the wealth gains from higher participation on average.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrolment 401(k) participants.
why_it_matters: The most detailed quantified evidence on default-level anchoring and multi-year persistence, directly bearing on the multiplier pre-selection decision, though in an employer-plan setting the brief flags as only an analogy.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) plan, not a self-directed consumer app
no discussion of the employer-trust mechanism's absence in our setting
classic (2001) data predating current fintech/regulatory context
relevance_reason: Most detailed quantified evidence on default-level anchoring (C3) and persistence (C2), capped by its employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Randomly assigning default enrolment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of thinking through savings scenarios rather than by trust in the payer, with effects on savings attitudes persisting after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees in Afghanistan with follow-on interventions isolating mechanisms behind the default effect.
why_it_matters: Directly tests why defaults work — present bias and cognitive cost, not employer-trust — speaking to the brief's core question of whether the default effect should be expected to transfer to a self-directed consumer app, and shows persistence of attitude change beyond the intervention.
limitations: salary-linked account for waged employees, a semi-employer-mediated setting rather than a fully self-directed consumer app
developing-country context differs from EU regulatory/liquidity context
abstract reports participation and attitude persistence, not amount saved
relevance_reason: Uniquely isolates the psychological mechanism behind default effects rather than employer trust, addressing whether the effect transfers to our non-employer setting.

key_finding: A field experiment with a consumer financial-management platform found payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, abstract-only for design details.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry that a uniform nudge/default can help most users while making a vulnerable subgroup worse off — exactly the distributional risk the brief says we must check before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
credit card/overdraft fee context rather than a round-up savings pot
no measure of long-run persistence beyond the fee outcomes reported
relevance_reason: Strong consumer-fintech evidence of heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects from a well-intentioned behavioural intervention, directly relevant to the brief's distributional-risk criterion.
